To rejoice/be delighted/be joyful
The idiom (including 19:26; 25:74; 28:9; 32:17, in which the expression ٌَيْعَأَْتَ رُق [“delight
of the eye’] is used) means literally: (of one’s eyes) to become cool. It is said that the tears
of joy are cool – whence the idiom – whereas the tears of sorrow are warm, and hence
the imprecation: َُهَنْيَعَُللّاََنَخْسَأMay God cause him sorrow [literally: may God make his
eyes war]!” But perhaps the two idioms can be explained in terms of one’s experience in
desert life: eyes warm from the blazing sun would be sore but in the evening, or in the
shade of a tree, the eyes would be restful.
It should be notes that the idiom under discussion is, in 20:40; 28:13; 33:51; and 19:26,
used in situations where pain, sorrow, or worry is followed by joy or happiness, thus
adding the meaning of relief to that of delight or pleasure.

رَطَو means “need,” and َىىضَقََُهَرَطَو to satisfy one’s need”. But the meaning of “need”
gives rise to that of “attachment”: if one needs something, one develops an attachment
for it. َىىضَقََُهَرَطَو  thus comes to mean “to sever one’s relations [with somebody],” for after
the fulfillment of the need the attachment is, or may be, lost. In the Qur’anic verse, the
use of the word رَطَو instead of قلَط divorce”) signifies that Zaynab (Zayd’s wife) had
completed her waiting period after the divorce, for, after the completion of the waiting
period, the connection between a man and his wife is completely severed. Zamakhshari
writes: انْعَملاََو :ََوَاهَقَ لَطََوَُهُسْفَنَاْنَعَْتَباتََوَُهُتَ م هَاْنَعَْتَرَساقَتََوٌَةَجاحَاْيْ فَ دْيَز لََقْبَيَْمَلَا مَلَف

Compare the construction in 69:3 (referred to as i) and 33:63 (referred to as ii):
i and ii are usually considered interchangeable, but the Quranic usage suggests that there

َىىَرْدَأ (دَرَيَas a verb with an object
َ
Compare the construction in 69:3 (referred to as i) and 33:63 (referred to as ii):
i and ii are usually considered interchangeable, but the Quranic usage suggests that there
is some difference between the two. First, i indicates the momentous or prodigious nature
of something, but that is not necessarily the case with ii. Second, i implies that the listener
either lacks all knowledge about the thing in question or is unaware of its true
significance, whereas ii implies that the listener may have formed some idea of what is
being talked about, but could be grossly mistaken in his estimation. Third, i takes the form
of an explication, but ii is in the form of a comment: ََكاَرْدَأَاَم is, in all the verses it occurs
in, regularly followed by a ََوُهَاَم construction, which paves the way for an explication of
the subject under discussion, thus suggesting that the gap in the listener's knowledge
needs to be filled; ََكْي رْدَيَاَمon the other hand, is in all cases followed by a اَذَكَُىَ للّاََ لَعَل
construction, implying that it is not necessary to fill the gap in the listener's knowledge,
though he should be warned of the error in the view he has formed of something. This
analysis is based on a study of the Quranic examples. It seems that the last of the three
conditions is not crucial as far as Arabic usage in general is concerned.

And what, do you think, is that? [literally: what would inform you as to what it is?]
Compare the construction in 69:3 (referred to as i) and 33:63 (referred to as ii):
i and ii are usually considered interchangeable, but the Quranic usage suggests that there
is some difference between the two. First, i indicates the momentous or prodigious nature
of something, but that is not necessarily the case with ii. Second, i implies that the listener
either lacks all knowledge about the thing in question or is unaware of its true
significance, whereas ii implies that the listener may have formed some idea of what is
being talked about, but could be grossly mistaken in his estimation. Third, i takes the form
of an explication, but ii is in the form of a comment: ََكاَرْدَأَاَم is, in all the verses it occurs
in, regularly followed by a ََوُهَاَم construction, which paves the way for an explication of
the subject under discussion, thus suggesting that the gap in the listener's knowledge
needs to be filled; ََكْي رْدَيَاَمon the other hand, is in all cases followed by a اَذَكَُ
ىَ للّاََ لَعَل
construction, implying that it is not necessary to fill the gap in the listener's knowledge,
though he should be warned of the error in the view he has formed of something. This
analysis is based on a study of the Quranic examples. It seems that the last of the three
conditions is not crucial as far as Arabic usage in general is concerned.

َىىَرْدَأ (دَرَيَas a verb with an object
ََوُهَاَمََكاَرْدَأَاَمَ
And what, do you think, is that? [literally: what would inform you as to what it is?]
Compare the construction in 69:3 (referred to as i) and 33:63 (referred to as ii):
i and ii are usually considered interchangeable, but the Quranic usage suggests that there
is some difference between the two. First, i indicates the momentous or prodigious nature
of something, but that is not necessarily the case with ii. Second, i implies that the listener
either lacks all knowledge about the thing in question or is unaware of its true
significance, whereas ii implies that the listener may have formed some idea of what is
being talked about, but could be grossly mistaken in his estimation. Third, i takes the form
of an explication, but ii is in the form of a comment: ََكاَرْدَأَاَم is, in all the verses it occurs
in, regularly followed by a ََوُهَاَم construction, which paves the way for an explication of
the subject under discussion, thus suggesting that the gap in the listener's knowledge
needs to be filled; ََكْي رْدَيَاَمon the other hand, is in all cases followed by a اَذَكَُ
ىَ للّاََ لَعَل
construction, implying that it is not necessary to fill the gap in the listener's knowledge,
though he should be warned of the error in the view he has formed of something. This
analysis is based on a study of the Quranic examples. It seems that the last of the three
conditions is not crucial as far as Arabic usage in general is concerned.
